title: A harsh consolation
hookLine: Seneca's letter to a grieving father is stern, and many readers find it too hard (Letters 99)

cards: Not every page of a great book deserves our agreement. For weeks, inside these letters, Seneca has been wise, funny and honest by turns. Today, some readers would say, he's none of those things.

A man named Marullus has lost a small son, and Seneca hears he's taking it very hard. So he writes him a letter, and sends a copy on to Lucilius, explaining that Marullus deserved a rebuke more than comfort.
Some readers wince. We'll read it honestly, and we're allowed to disagree.

teach.b: First, the opening. Do you expect comfort? Seneca asks the grieving father, more or less.
You'll get a scolding. He tells Marullus he's bearing a small loss badly, and even calls his grief unmanly, in the language of his time. Second, the arguments.
The boy was very young, Seneca says; you hadn't had time to know what he would become. Think of what you had, not what you lost.

teach.h: HE WAS SO YOUNG; YOU KNEW HE WAS MORTAL.
teach.b: Everyone dies; you knew he was mortal. Some of this echoes letter sixty-three. Here, though, it comes without warmth, to a father, about a child.
Third, what Seneca allows. Later in the letter he softens a little.

Tears that fall by themselves, at the first news or at the funeral, are natural, he says, and nobody should be blamed for them. What he attacks is grief performed for an audience, kept going because people are watching.
Fourth, where we part ways. Some readers, including some who love Seneca, find this letter too hard. To a parent, a small child's death is not a small loss.

And Seneca himself confessed, in letter sixty-three, that he wept for Serenus beyond his own rule. The Stoic idea that grief shouldn't swallow a life may be wise. But the way you say it to a father matters.
Learning from a teacher includes knowing where to be gentler than he was.

how: Some modern readers of Seneca keep his warning against performed, endless grief while choosing a gentler way to comfort the grieving than his letter to Marullus.

games.q: a friend has lost a child and is overwhelmed. you've read Seneca's letter to Marullus. what do you do?
o: send them Seneca's letter word for word.
keep his point about performed grief to yourself, and comfort gently.
tell them the loss was small.
games.why: the letter has a real insight, but some readers part ways with its tone: today's line is gentler than Seneca.

practice: Think of someone you know who is hurting right now, a loss, a diagnosis, a disappointment, and notice if any part of you wants to fix them or hurry them along. Let that soften.
Imagine sitting beside them and saying very little: I'm here, I'm so sorry, take your time.

wordCard.voice: Consolatio. The Roman genre of consolation letter: Seneca's to Marullus is stern, sometimes wise, and for some readers too hard. A place to be gentler than he was. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: consolation, a Roman genre of letter or essay; Seneca also wrote consolations to Marcia, to Polybius and to his mother Helvia.

carryVoice: Your line: gentler than seneca. Comfort can come gently, with no lecture at all. See you tomorrow.
